lines.note: Honegumi no tsuyoi hito ja: a person of strong build. This continues the bone-frame entry from f208; initial f represents Japanese h, not an error to modernize.
Forte e rijo describes strength and toughness. The second Japanese example starts takumashii across ta-/cumaxij, so the physical break is not a lexical boundary.
Takumashii hito, a robust or muscular person, agrees with membrudo. The final ij belongs to the historical spelling of the adjective.
Hōnen, a plentiful harvest year, is glossed yutakana toshi. The Portuguese abundant adjective begins with a- here and continues on the next row.
Kotoshi wa hōnen ja says that this is a fruitful year. Read bundante to complete abundante, not the OCR's bandante; the next definition begins Es-/te.

runs.text: te anno he proſpero, & de nouidade.

lines.note: This year is prosperous and productive. The scan supports prospero rather than prostero; nouidade here concerns produce or the harvest, not simply a modern novelty.
Honenami concerns the arrangement of bones; shishiai introduces flesh or bodily conformation in the horse example. The definition is anatomical rather than a reference to literal waves.

The example continues the description of a horse's conformation. I retain the printed yomeno fuxi rather than guessing a modern anatomical expression; its exact lexical interpretation remains uncertain.
Tsukuri-tsuketaru gotoku nari compares the horse to something perfectly fashioned. Portuguese proporcionado crosses the line; the internal OCR space in proporciona- is unsupported.

runs.text: do, & de boas feiçoẽs como ſe o fizerão ao tor

lines.note: As if made on a lathe: como se o fizerão ao torno. The magnified scan supports se and fizerão; retain the historical verb ending rather than modernizing its syntax.
Completes torno and the comparison with the shape one desires. There is no reason to create a Japanese word from this short Portuguese continuation.
Hone-tsugai, joints of the bones. The plural masculine ossos fits both the scan and juntas; oßas was an OCR vowel error.
Hongaku, Buddhist original enlightenment, is represented here through a missionary description of primordial substance. Bup. is an upright Buddhist vocabulary label, not part of the headword.

runs.text: principio, ou Fotoque ãtes deſe misturar no cor-

lines.note: The gloss describes a Fotoque before entering bodily life. Principio, Fotoque and ãtes are visible; misturar contains a t, not an ss ligature. These are transcription repairs, not an endorsement of the theological description.
Cor-/po completes corpo, followed by living. The physical line belongs to the preceding Buddhist definition.
Honji, the original ground or substance, is another Buddhist term. The damaged label is Bup., not Buo.; Fotoque remains italic as printed in this explanation.

runs.text: antes de ſefazer Cami & ſer venerado nalgũa

lines.note: The original being precedes its manifestation as a kami and its veneration in a shrine. Preserve the close printed sefazer rather than silently regularizing Portuguese spacing.
Honji suijaku, 本地垂迹, identifies the doctrine behind the preceding explanation. Suixacu is a historically intelligible spelling; Idem refers back to that gloss.
Honjin, the principal army or headquarters, is analyzed as hon no jin. Unlike the preceding honji entry, this is a military rather than Buddhist definition.

runs.text: eſta o principal capitão, ou general.

lines.note: The chief captain or general is stationed there. Principal replaces prencipal; the printed accent is retained on capitão after comparison with the visible word.

runs.text: Texto, ou autoridade de algum texto.

lines.note: Hongo here denotes an authoritative text or quotation. This sense must be kept distinct from the homograph in the next entry.
Hongo wo hiku means citing a text. Fiqu corresponds to hiku, and alegar is adducing authority rather than merely making an allegation.
The second Fongo points to Fôgu, scrap paper. The magnified cross-reference reads Fôgu, not Fiǒgu; the Portuguese explicitly introduces a spelling/pronunciation distinction.
Although written fongo, it is pronounced fōgu. The whole repeated Japanese word is upright, and the scan shows aßi and pronunciaſe. Keep the printed papeisborrados spacing.
Hongoku, one's original country, is explained by moto no kuni. The Portuguese kingdom is one's own or native realm in this context.
Completes the native-country definition: where someone was born. Naceo is retained as printed rather than updated to modern nasceu.
Hongwai, 本懐, satisfaction or the fulfilment of a wish. The historical labialized spelling is meaningful; italic S. belongs to the Portuguese explanation.
Hongwai ni zonji sōrō expresses pleasure or satisfaction. The scan supports Fonguaini, not Fonguami; ni is the particle required by the construction.

runs.text: & folgo muito. ¶ Item, Deſejo, ou von-

lines.note: The speaker rejoices greatly. Item then introduces the related nominal sense of desire or wish, with vontade divided across rows.
Hongwai ni kanō, to have one's wishes fulfilled. Canǒ is the historical contracted form corresponding to kanau; the Portuguese explicitly confirms fulfilment.
Completes the Portuguese object, desires. This is a continuation, not a new entry or a heading.

runs.text: Proprio voto como o de Amida.

lines.note: Hongwan, 本願, the original vow, exemplified by Amida's. Amida is part of the italic Portuguese explanation here.

runs.text: ¶ Item, Aliquando, O que edifica, ou

lines.note: Aliquando introduces another occasional sense: the person who builds or founds something. It is Latin explanatory vocabulary, not a Japanese reading.

runs.text: funda algũa Tera à ſua cuſta principalmente,

lines.note: Someone founds a tera at their own expense. Read funda and sua, not fanda and sus; the borrowed temple word stays in the printed italic setting.

runs.text: posto que a propria palaura he,

lines.note: The writer qualifies this usage: the more proper term is hongwannin, 本願人. This is why the same longer headword receives a cross-reference below.
A further sense denotes the first superior of a temple. Fonguan is repeated as the word under discussion, not a new independent heading.

runs.text: edificou algũa Tera, ou algum ſeu ſocceſor q̃

lines.note: The founding superior or a successor who governs the temple. Preserve the historical soccesor-type spelling rather than substituting modern sucessor.
The successor governs in the founder's place. The short continuation completes the preceding relative clause.
Hongwannin refers back to hongwan. The nn spelling is compatible with gw an plus nin; it is not an accidental duplicated consonant to remove.
Honguen, 本源, source or origin, is explained by moto and minamoto. These Japanese equivalents agree directly with principio.

Hongeki denotes rebellion or treachery. The example ends in vokosu on the next row. The connector in Fongueqino is worn and retained after enlargement; an expected accusative -uo is not enough by itself to replace it.
Completes vokosu and the Portuguese armar traição, plotting treachery. The scan shows a cedilla in traição; this is not merely modern spelling normalization.
Hongui, 本義, is an original or legitimate matter, explained as hon no koto. The i marker introduces an explanation rather than contributing Japanese syllables.

runs.text: tima couſa. ¶ Item, Couſa antigua, & q̃

lines.note: The second sense is something ancient or original. Antigua is retained as historical Portuguese; the following Latin phrase continues the explanation.

runs.text: ab initio aßi auia de ſer.

lines.note: Ab initio, from the beginning: it had originally been so. Read initio aßi auia, recovering the obscured letters rather than the OCR's intio aß auta.
Hongyaku, 反逆, is equated with hongeki and glossed somuku, sakashima. The l is an alternative marker, not part of a Japanese word.
Traição completes the rebellion entry. The library stamp overlaps this short row, but the word and its descender remain readable in the crop.

runs.text: Proprio texto, ou liuro da ley eſẽ-

lines.note: Hongyō, a principal scriptural text. Liuro is visibly the intended Portuguese noun, not liaro; the open-o diacritic on the Japanese heading remains as read by OCR.
Completes essencial, qualifying the religious text. No omitted new heading is implied by this short continuation.
Hon-i, 本意, one's true intention or meaning, is explained as hon no kokoro. The internal hyphen distinguishes the vowel following n and is retained.
Hon-i wo somuku means going against the proper intention or reason. The Portuguese discrepancy verb begins Des here, without an added line-end hyphen.

runs.text: crepar do que he razão, & corteſia. ¶ Itẽ,

lines.note: Completes discrepar/descrepar: departing from reason and courtesy. Keep the historical printed vowel and division rather than substituting the modern verb.
Hon-i ni naru, to attain one's desire. The Portuguese Com continues as comprir on the next row; do not manufacture a missing hyphen.
Completes the gloss: to fulfil one's wishes or will. Comprir is a historical spelling and is not an OCR error solely because cumprir is familiar today.
Honja, 本社, the main shrine, is explained as hon no yashiro. The Portuguese ermida is the missionaries' comparison for the shrine building.

runs.text: caſa do Cami em reſpeito doutras inferiores.

lines.note: The principal house of the kami relative to lesser shrines. The magnified word is Cami, not cumi, and respeito contains the lost e; Cami is italic in this explanation.

runs.text: Voto, ou juramento como o que fez

lines.note: Honzei, 本誓, a vow or oath. Je represents the historical voiced sibilant here; it should not be read with a modern English j sound.
Amida and other Fotoques are the examples of beings making such vows. Both borrowed names appear in the italic explanatory text.

runs.text: Meſa principal com comer. i, A q̃

lines.note: Honzen, 本膳, the principal meal tray. Portuguese mesa com comer is a table or tray with food, not an abstract main meal alone.
The tray bears rice and xiru, soup. The magnified scan places the whole Xiru in italic; a roman X alone was an OCR style-boundary artifact.
Honzet, 本説, authentic teaching, explained as hon no setsu. The final t is the period's word-final notation and should not be expanded in the diplomatic text.
Another sense is true news. Na pratica introduces a usage note about the spoken or ordinary form, continued below.
Fonxet is the practical form; Fixet is its opposite, false or unfounded news. These contrasted Japanese forms are upright within the Portuguese sentence.
Honji, 本寺, the principal temple, compared with a mother church. This is not the preceding Buddhist 本地 despite the similar modern pronunciation.
Honjin, 本心, fundamental mind or one's true senses, explained by konbon no shin. The scan's Conbonuo is retained as the period's linked spelling.

runs.text: q̃ ſe trata no Buppô. ¶ Item, Proprio ſer,

lines.note: The first sense is discussed in Buddhist doctrine, Buppô. Read q̃ ſe trata: the faint long s was mistaken for d and joined to q̃. Buppô is wholly italic here.
Honjin wo ushinō, losing one's senses. The final marked o belongs to the historical verb form corresponding to ushinau, not to a Portuguese word.

runs.text: der o juizo, ou eſtar fora de ſi cõ bebedice, &c.

lines.note: The example means losing one's judgement or being beside oneself through drunkenness. Bebedice is not to be replaced by a modern synonym.
Honjo is an original document. Keep this short homograph separate from the longer place/landholding entry below.
Honjo, 本所, begins with the original or former place, moto no tokoro. The Portuguese anti-/guo is divided across the physical rows.
Honjo ye kaeru means returning to one's former place. Ye is the directional particle and cayeru is the historical romanization of kaeru.

runs.text: a ſeu primeiro, ou antigo lugar. ¶ Item,

lines.note: Completes returning to the former place. The scan here reads antigo rather than the OCR's split a ntiguo; retain variation from anti-/guo immediately above.

runs.text: Nome de Cigues ordinarios: vſaſe ſempre

lines.note: Another sense is a designation for ordinary Cigues. This court-related borrowed term is kept as printed; a precise rank equivalence should not be inferred solely from ordinarios.
The title is used with honorific go, hence gohonjo. A new example begins with gohonjo no kura, continuing below.

runs.text: Sella que fez hum official inſigne

lines.note: Gohonjo no kura is a saddle attributed to a renowned craftsman. The scan supports hum official insigne; the missing g was badly faded, not a genuine space inside the adjective.
The craftsman is called Ixedono, Ise-dono; the saddle suits any horse. Keep the personal designation upright as printed and do not modernize its xe spelling.
A Kami-region usage of Fonjo then means the landlord. No Cami belongs wholly to the italic Portuguese note; Fonjo is upright, rather than the OCR's split Ca ni, Fonji.

runs.text: nhorio a quem pagam o foro dalgum chão,

lines.note: The landlord receives the foro, a due or ground rent, for land. This is a social/legal gloss, not a second physical place example.
Or houses: the short row finishes the rental-property definition. It remains body text rather than page furniture.
A further Honjo means the first beginning, with moto and hajime as equivalents. The different homographs are not merged by their identical spelling.
Honmaru, 本丸, the principal castle enclosure. Castello is retained with the OCR's short s; meaning supplies no reason to change that allograph.

runs.text: mais interior onde mora o ſenhor, ou capitão em

lines.note: The innermost enclosure houses the lord or captain. This narrows the previous general fortress gloss to the main residential/defensive enclosure.

runs.text: reſpeito de outras cercas, & caſtellos menos

lines.note: It is contrasted with other outer works and lesser castles. Cercas here denotes enclosures, not merely generic fences in isolation.

runs.text: principaes que eſtão dentro da meſma fortaleza

lines.note: Those secondary enclosures are within the same overall fortress. Principaes and fortaleza retain their historical spellings.
Vniuersal completes the sense of the fortress as a whole. It is a Portuguese continuation, not a separate universal concept entry.
Honmat, 本末, beginning and end, glossed moto and sue. The initial damaged capital is F, not ſ; the Japanese meaning independently supports the headword identification.
Hyōshi no honmatsu wo totonoete: arranging the beginning and end of the rhythm or performance. The final t in the headword expands before the following particle here.
The Portuguese describes tuning or coordinating instruments. Concertando includes the faint t, omitted by OCR; it does not refer to a different verb concerar.

runs.text: inſtrumentos que concorde principio com fim.

lines.note: The instruments should agree from beginning to end. Read instrumentos rather than instramentos; preserve the printed singular concorde rather than silently correcting grammar.
Honmyaku, 本脈, the normal pulse. Ordinario begins with o, not c; the Japanese and Portuguese meanings coincide straightforwardly.
Honmō, 本望, a wish; honmō wo toguru means fulfilling it. The caron is retained rather than replacing it from a modern long-vowel convention.
Tassuru is an alternative verb for attaining one's desire. Both long s characters are independently visible in this upright Japanese sequence.
Honmon, 本文, the proper or original text. Proprio replaces the OCR's Progrio, confirmed by the printed p and the definition.
Honnin, 本人, the principal person, glossed moto hito. Read prin- rather than prim,; f210 begins with cipal and completes principal. The repeated cipal at this page's foot is a catchword.

Previously misclassified as body text; its stable ID is retained. Its repetition at the start of f210 establishes that this is a catchword, despite its position inside the lower rule beside the signature. The descending final l is not an additional full stop.
